question:
**Directions: Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.**

To have an axe to grind

options.text: To have adequate means of subsistence
To have an indomitable task to accomplish
To have a selfish motive in doing something
To have access to top levels of authority

solution:
The correct answer is '**To have a selfish motive in doing something**.'

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Given Idiom: ***To have an axe to grind*** means To have a selfish motive in doing something. (कुछ करने का स्वार्थी मकसद होना)

 
 
• Example:* Some new reports may be biased because the reporters **have an axe to grind***.
 
 
 
• From the given options, the third option is the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

 

Hence, the correct answer is option 3.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e085a7f17645c801966c030eb44d69fae944b96fdb4c4077f5fba1bc2c24bc71.png] **Mistake Points__**

__
 
• We may think from the phrase "To have an axe to grind" that it is all about having an indomitable task to accomplish.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• *The phrase is used with the meaning “having ulterior motive” in America and “having a dispute to take or point of view to express” in Britain. The phrase, with the American meaning, is commonly attributed to Benjamin Franklin. Two of his works from 1771 to 1790 have similar references, but the exact phrase is not present. In some opinions, the phrase is attributed to Charles Miner, who, like Franklin, lived in Pennsylvania, USA. Miner was the first to have the exact phrase in print, in two similar articles in 1810 and 1812.*
